intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13; the Gita Press viniyoga at the head of chapter 5 calls it the uttara-caritra). In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga, not a statement of the Purāṇa text. The pāṭha also sets a dhyāna before this chapter, of Padmāvatī — seated on the lord of serpents, three-eyed, bright as the sun, holding rosary, water-pot, skull and lotus, crowned with the half-moon, resting in the lap of Bhairava, the all-knowing lord. That meditation belongs to the liturgy; the chapter itself does not mention it.
intro.summary: Medhas takes up the story where chapter 5 left it (6.1). The messenger, seething with indignation, reports the Devī’s words to Śumbha in full (6.2). Śumbha, enraged, orders Dhūmralocana, a commander of the daityas, to take his own army and bring her by force, dragged helpless by the hair (6.3–4), and to kill anyone — god, yakṣa or gandharva — who comes forward to protect her (6.5). Dhūmralocana sets off at once with sixty thousand asuras (6.6–7), finds the Devī on the snowy mountain, and shouts at her to go to Śumbha and Niśumbha willingly or be dragged there by the hair (6.8–9). The Devī answers with a single ironic verse: if a strong man, sent by the lord of the daityas and surrounded by an army, takes her by force, what can she do to him? (6.10–11). He rushes at her, and Ambikā burns him to ashes with the sound ‘huṃ’ alone (6.12–13). She showers his furious army with arrows, spears and axes (6.14); her lion, mane tossing and roaring, falls upon it and kills with paw, jaws, claws and the flat of the paw, beheading some and drinking the blood of others (6.15–18), until in a moment the whole army is destroyed (6.19). Hearing that the Devī has slain Dhūmralocana and her lion his army, Śumbha, his lip trembling, orders Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa to take a great force and bring her, dragged by the hair or bound; if that is in doubt, to have all the asuras strike her down with every weapon; and, when she and her lion are felled, to bind her and come back (6.20–24).
intro.forms: The Devī (देवी, 6.2, 6.8, 6.20) and Ambikā (6.13, 6.14, 6.24) — the Ambikā who came forth from Pārvatī’s body and is sung as Kauśikī (5.87) — still abiding on Himālaya (6.8); the speaker of one ironic verse (6.11); the one whose ‘huṃ’ burns an asura to ash (6.13); the warrior who rains arrows, spears and axes (6.14); and, through her lion, ‘the Devī’s own mount’ (6.15, 6.19, 6.20), the destroyer of an army. The asuras’ names for her — ‘that insolent one’ (दुष्टा, 6.4, 6.24), the polite ‘lady’ (भवती, 6.9) — are their view of her, not hers. Padmāvatī, of the dhyāna, is the form of the liturgy, not of the text.
intro.significance: This is the first of the envoys sent against the Devī after her challenge in chapter 5 (5.120–121): Dhūmralocana, then Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (chapter 7), then Raktabīja (chapter 8), and finally Niśumbha and Śumbha themselves. Each defeat brings a stronger force and a harsher order. The chapter turns on a contrast of scale: sixty thousand asuras and their general (6.7) against one syllable (6.13) and one lion (6.19). Śumbha’s orders also change in the course of it — from ‘bring her’ (6.4) to ‘if it is in doubt, strike her down’ (6.23) — and they end in contradiction (6.24).
intro.grammar: A short narrative chapter: reduplicated perfects (ययौ, जगाद, पपात, जघान, पपौ, चुकोप) beside periphrastic perfects (पाटयामास, 6.17; आज्ञापयामास, 6.21); chains of absolutives leading to one finite verb (6.2, 6.3, 6.8, 6.20); conditional sentences of several shapes (यदि … सः, 6.5; न … चेत् … ततः, 6.9; an implied condition answered by ततः, 6.11; यदि … तदा, 6.23); passive participles with an instrumental agent (6.18, 6.19, 6.20); a double accusative with कृ (तं भस्म चकार, 6.13); commands put in the passive (समानीयताम्, 6.22; विनिहन्यताम्, 6.23) and the impersonal passive (आगम्यताम्, 6.24); and a locative absolute (तस्यां हतायाम्, 6.24). Sentences run across verses at 6.20–21 and 6.22–23.
intro.teaching: Literally, a king sends a general to seize a woman; she burns him with a syllable, her lion destroys his army, and the king sends two more. As teaching, the chapter shows what force cannot do. The asuras speak only of strength — बल is army and violence at once (6.4, 6.9, 6.11) — and imagine that she can be defended only by someone else (6.5); the Goddess needs no one, and her power is so far beyond theirs that a sound is enough (6.13). Read devotionally, ‘huṃ’ is heard as her own sound acting as her weapon, and her lion as her power acting through what belongs to her; that reading is the tradition’s, not a statement of the verse. A modern reflection: the wish to possess, refused, turns to rage and then to the wish to destroy (6.9, 6.23).
themes: Force against power: the army and the syllable
The hair-dragging order: the asura will to possess
The Devī’s lion: her own protector

conclusion.narrative: Śumbha does not answer the Devī’s challenge himself. He sends Dhūmralocana with sixty thousand asuras and the order to drag her back by the hair. She asks, with irony, what a lone woman could do against such strength; then a single ‘huṃ’ turns the general to ash, and her lion, in a moment, destroys his army. The chapter ends not with the battle but with Śumbha’s next and harsher order, to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa: bring her, or strike her down (6.21–24).

constructions: Absolutives leading to one finite verb (इत्याकर्ण्य … समागम्य … समाचष्ट, 6.2; दृष्ट्वा … जगाद, 6.8).
Conditionals: यदि … सः हन्तव्यः (6.5), न चेत् … ततः (6.9), an implied condition answered by ततः (6.11), यदि … तदा (6.23).
Double accusative with कृ: तं भस्म चकार, ‘made him ash’ (6.13).
Passive participle with an instrumental agent: तेन … कृताः (6.18), केसरिणा क्षयं नीतम् (6.19), देव्या निहतम् (6.20).
Commands in the passive (समानीयताम्, 6.22; विनिहन्यताम्, 6.23) and the impersonal passive of an intransitive verb (आगम्यताम्, 6.24).
The locative absolute: तस्यां हतायां … सिंहे च विनिपातिते, ‘when she has been struck down and the lion felled’ (6.24).
The periphrastic perfect of -aya stems (पाटयामास, 6.17; आज्ञापयामास, 6.21) beside the reduplicated perfect (ययौ, पपौ, जघान).
सः and एषः drop their visarga before a consonant (स दूतः, 6.2; एष केशा-, 6.9), but before a they follow the ordinary rule (सोऽभ्यधावत्, 6.13).
insights: The Devī needs no instrument against the asura’s general: one syllable, ‘huṃ’, is enough (6.13), and the word एव ‘alone’ carries the point. Devotees hear her sound itself as her power.
The protector Śumbha expects to come from outside — a god, a yakṣa, a gandharva (6.5) — is already hers: ‘the Devī’s own mount’ (6.15, 6.19). She depends on no other being.
The asuras think in terms of बल; the Devī turns the word back on them three times in one verse (6.11) and answers it with a power of another order (6.13).

The Goddess cannot be ‘brought’: three times the asuras demand that she be taken by force (6.4, 6.9, 6.22–24), and she stays where she is, on the mountain (6.8). Her own condition was that only the one who conquers her in battle may claim her (5.120).
The wish to possess her turns, when refused, into the wish to destroy her: from ‘my master’ (6.9) to ‘let all the asuras strike her down’ (6.23).
conclusion.srividya: Two names of the Devī in this chapter are also names in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Ambikā (295, अम्बिका), the name used for her here at 6.13, 6.14 and 6.24, and Daityahantrī (599, दैत्यहन्त्री, ‘slayer of daityas’), which names what the chapter shows. The Lalitā Sahasranāma also tells of the Goddess’s forces destroying an asura army — Bhaṇḍāsura’s (65, 72) — but that is a different myth, and the likeness is one of pattern, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The ‘huṃ’ of 6.13 is a syllable of general mantra practice, not of Śrīvidyā in particular. No specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: Śumbha’s order: take your army and bring that insolent woman by force, dragged helpless by the hair.
The Devī’s only speech: sent by the daitya lord, strong, with an army — if you take me by force, what can I do to you?
Dhūmralocana rushes at her, and Ambikā burns him to ashes with the sound ‘huṃ’ alone.
The Devī’s own mount, the lion, shakes its mane, roars, and falls upon the asura army.
In a moment the whole army is destroyed by the lion, the Devī’s furious mount.
Śumbha to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa: drag her by the hair or bind her; if the fight is in doubt, let all the asuras strike her down.

grammar_notes: Two sentences run across verses: 6.20 is an absolutive clause whose main verb is चुकोप in 6.21; 6.23 completes the order of 6.22. The anvayas say so.
क्षयितम् (6.20) is an unusual participle, kept as printed and analysed from a stem क्षयय-; देव्या there is read as the instrumental agent of निहतम्.
गच्छत (6.22) is plural though two are addressed (the dual would be गच्छतम्).
अधरेण (6.16) is taken as ‘with the lower jaw’; हतायाम् (6.24) as ‘struck down’, not ‘killed’, because she is then to be bound and brought.
प्राह (6.3) is used as a narrative past; उत्तिष्ठते (6.5) takes the ātmanepada for ‘to come forward’; आज्ञप्तः (6.7) is formed from the short causative stem ज्ञप्-.
themes: The lion as the Devī’s own
uncertain: No variant reading is recorded for this chapter in corrections.json.
Interpretive doubts are flagged on 6.16 (अधरेण: lower jaw or hind parts), 6.20 (the form क्षयितम्; देव्या as instrumental) and 6.24 (हता: struck down or slain). None doubts the printed reading.

mantras.lit: Having heard thus the words of the Devī, that messenger, filled with indignation, having come back, reported (them) in detail to the king of the daityas.
mantras.tr: When he had heard these words of the Devī, the messenger, seething with indignation, went back and told the king of the daityas everything at length.

comm.t: The messenger is Sugrīva (5.102). What he reports is the Devī’s vow — whoever conquers her in battle and matches her strength will be her husband (5.120) — and her invitation to Śumbha or Niśumbha to come and win her (5.121, 5.129). His anger is the anger of a servant whose master has been slighted.

The uttama-carita moves by escalation: after the messenger come Dhūmralocana (this chapter), Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (chapter 7), Raktabīja (chapter 8), and finally Niśumbha and Śumbha themselves. Each refusal brings a stronger envoy.

mantras.tr: When the lord of the asuras heard the messenger’s report, he flew into a rage and said to Dhūmralocana, a commander of the daityas:

comm.t: Śumbha does not answer the Devī’s challenge himself; he sends a commander. The chapter’s Gita Press colophon calls Dhūmralocana a general (सेनानी) of Śumbha and Niśumbha; his name means ‘he whose eyes are smoke-coloured’.
A modern reading, not a traditional one: the ‘smoke-eyed’ general is sent to seize what he cannot see clearly. The text itself says nothing of the name’s meaning.

mantras.anvaya: हे धूम्रलोचन, स्वसैन्यपरिवारितः त्वम् आशु ताम् दुष्टाम् केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम् बलात् आनय।
mantras.anvaya_en: Vocative, subject with its participle phrase, the imperative आनय with its object ताम् दुष्टाम् and the predicate adjective केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम्; बलात् gives the manner.
mantras.lit: O Dhūmralocana, you, surrounded by your own army, bring quickly by force that wicked one, distraught from the dragging of her hair.
mantras.tr: Dhūmralocana, take your army and bring that insolent woman here at once — by force, dragged helpless by the hair.
mantras.tr_note: केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम् describes the state in which she is to arrive; the tr turns it into a phrase of manner.

comm.t: Śumbha takes up the threat his messenger had already made (5.126: केशाकर्षणनिर्धूतगौरवा, ‘your dignity shaken off by being dragged by the hair’). The phrase केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम् returns in Dhūmralocana’s mouth (6.9), and the order to drag her by the hair is repeated to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (6.23).

To drag a woman by the hair is, in the epic world, the sign of the worst outrage — it is what is done to Draupadī in the Mahābhārata’s assembly hall. By making it his order, Śumbha shows the listener what kind of power he is.

mantras.anvaya_en: A conditional clause (यदि … उत्तिष्ठते) and its main clause (सः हन्तव्यः); the three classes of being (अमरः वा अपि यक्षः गन्धर्वः एव वा) say who the protector might be.
mantras.lit: And if any other, giving her protection, rises up — he is to be killed, whether he be an immortal, or even a yakṣa, or a gandharva.
mantras.tr: And if anyone else comes forward to protect her — god, yakṣa or gandharva — kill him.

comm.t: Śumbha imagines that the woman can only be defended by someone else — a god, a yakṣa, a gandharva — the very beings he has already conquered (5.86, 5.107–111). The protector who does rise up is her own lion (6.15), and the power he does not imagine is hers (6.13).

mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (सः दैत्यः धूम्रलोचनः) with two participles (तेन आज्ञप्तः, … वृतः), two adverbs of speed and the verb ययौ.
mantras.lit: Commanded by him, then that daitya Dhūmralocana, surrounded by sixty thousand asuras, went swiftly, quickly.
mantras.tr: So commanded, the daitya Dhūmralocana set off at once and marched in haste, with sixty thousand asuras around him.
mantras.tr_note: The two adverbs of speed (शीघ्रम्, द्रुतम्) are given one each to ‘set off’ and ‘marched’.

comm.t: Dhūmralocana obeys immediately; the doubled ‘swiftly … quickly’ (शीघ्रम् … द्रुतम्) marks his haste. Sixty thousand asuras go with him — the first of the armies the Devī will face in this carita.

mantras.tr: When he saw the Devī standing on the snowy mountain, he called out loudly: “Go to Śumbha and Niśumbha!”
mantras.tr_note: मूलम् ‘to the foot of, the presence of’ is rendered simply ‘to’.

mantras.lit: If you, lady, do not today willingly go to my master, then I here take (you) by force, distraught from the dragging of your hair.
mantras.tr: If you will not come to my master willingly now, then I will take you there by force, dragged helpless by the hair.

comm.t: Dhūmralocana repeats his king’s order almost word for word (6.4: बलात्, केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम्). He offers only one choice: come willingly or be dragged. The Devī has already said what the condition is — whoever conquers her in battle (5.120).

mantras.anvaya: दैत्येश्वरेण प्रहितः बलवान् बलसंवृतः (त्वम्) एवं मां बलात् नयसि (चेत्), ततः अहं ते किं करोमि?
mantras.anvaya_en: The first clause has no यदि; the condition is implied and answered by ततः. The subject ‘you’ is carried by the verb नयसि and its three qualifiers (प्रहितः, बलवान्, बलसंवृतः).
mantras.lit: Sent by the lord of the daityas, mighty, surrounded by an army — (if) you thus take me by force, then what do I do to you?
mantras.tr: You were sent by the lord of the daityas; you are strong, and you have an army with you. If you take me by force like this, what can I do to you?
mantras.tr_note: The condition is implied in the Sanskrit (no यदि); ‘if’ is supplied from the correlative ततः.

comm.t: The Devī’s answer is ironic. She plays on बल three times — बलवान् ‘strong’, बलसंवृतः ‘with an army’, बलात् ‘by force’ — and asks what she, a lone woman, could do. The next verse answers her question.

The tradition reads such speeches as the Goddess’s play (līlā): in the fifth chapter she likewise calls her vow the fruit of ‘little understanding’ (5.119, अल्पबुद्धित्वात्), drawing the asuras into the battle that will end them.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the asura’s charge (subject, object ताम्, verb अभ्यधावत्), and the Devī’s answer (subject सा अम्बिका, instrument हुंकारेण एव, double accusative तं भस्म, verb चकार).
mantras.lit: Thus addressed, that asura Dhūmralocana rushed at her. Then she, Ambikā, made him ash with the sound ‘huṃ’ alone.
mantras.tr: At these words the asura Dhūmralocana rushed at her; and Ambikā, with nothing more than the sound ‘huṃ’, burned him to ashes.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Burned to ashes’ renders भस्म चकार ‘made (him) ash’.

comm.t: This verse answers her question in 6.11. The man who came to drag her away with sixty thousand soldiers is undone by one syllable; एव ‘alone, merely’ carries the point. The Devī has used her हुंकार before: in 3.12 Ambikā strikes down a hurled spear with it (हुंकाराभिहताम्).

In mantra practice हुं is a syllable of wrath and protection; in the six-limbed nyāsa it is the ending of the ‘armour’ limb (कवचाय हुम्). Devotees hear in this verse the Goddess’s sound itself as her weapon.
A modern reflection: the one who meets force with force needs an army; the one in whom power rests needs only a syllable. The asura’s display of strength is answered by stillness.

Past participle of √क्रुध्: dh + t → ddh. The army is angry at the death of its general.

mantras.lit: Then Ambikā likewise rained upon the enraged great army of the asuras with sharp arrows, and also with spears and axes.
mantras.tr: Then Ambikā showered the furious host of the asuras with sharp arrows, with spears and with axes.

comm.t: The general is ash; his army, enraged, remains. Against the army the Devī uses weapons — arrows, spears and axes — where against its leader a syllable was enough.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देव्याः स्ववाहनः सिंहः कोपात् धुतसटः सुभैरवं नादं कृत्वा असुरसेनायां पपात।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (सिंहः with देव्याः स्ववाहनः and the epithet धुतसटः), cause (कोपात्), the absolutive phrase (सुभैरवं नादं कृत्वा), place (असुरसेनायाम्), verb (पपात).
mantras.lit: Then the lion, the Devī’s own mount, with mane shaken, out of anger, having made a most terrible roar, fell upon the army of the asuras.
mantras.tr: Then the lion, the Devī’s own mount, shook its mane in fury, let out a terrible roar, and fell upon the asura army.

comm.t: The lion enters. It is the mount Himavat gave the Devī in the second chapter (2.29), and it fought there too ‘with tossing mane’ (2.68, धुतकेसरः). Śumbha had expected a protector — god, yakṣa or gandharva (6.5); the one who rises up is the Devī’s own lion.

Absolutive in -य of आ + √क्रम् ‘to step upon, attack’: here the lion leaps on and pins down its prey.
Perfect of √हन्: reduplication ज- with h → gh in the root after it (ज-घान), and vṛddhi of the root vowel in the 3rd singular.

mantras.anvaya: सः (सिंहः) कांश्चित् दैत्यान् करप्रहारेण, अपरान् च आस्येन, अन्यान् च आक्रम्य अधरेण, (एवं) महासुरान् जघान।
mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (जघान) with three objects, each paired with its instrument — कांश्चित् … करप्रहारेण, अपरान् … आस्येन, अन्यान् … अधरेण — and महासुरान् summing them up.
mantras.lit: Some daityas with a blow of his paw, others with his mouth, and others, having pounced on (them), with his lower jaw — he slew the great asuras.
mantras.tr: He slew the great asuras: some with a blow of his paw, others with his jaws, and others he pinned down and killed with his lower jaw.

comm.t: The lion fights as a lion fights: paw, jaws, the weight of its body. The next three verses go on with the same catalogue of carnage until the army is gone (6.19).

flags.uncertain: अधरेण: अधर is ‘the lower lip’ (as in प्रस्फुरिताधरः, 6.21), taken here as the lower jaw, so that the lion pins its prey and bites. Because आस्येन ‘with the mouth’ has just been used, some translators take अधर in its other sense, ‘the lower part (of the body)’, and read आक्रम्य … अधरेण as trampling with the hind parts. The reading itself is not in doubt.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses with the one subject केसरी: the first with the periphrastic perfect पाटयामास, the second with the participle कृतवान् and its predicate पृथक्.
mantras.lit: The maned one tore open with his claws the bellies of some; likewise with a blow of his paw he made heads separate.
mantras.tr: With his claws the lion ripped open the bellies of some; with blows of his paw he struck off heads.

comm.t: The catalogue goes on: claws for the belly, the flat of the paw for the head. The text calls the lion केसरी, ‘the maned one’, from here to 6.20.

samasa.sense: with tossing mane, the same epithet as in 2.68

morph.note: Past passive participle with the agent in the instrumental (तेन) and a predicate nominative (विच्छिन्नबाहुशिरसः): ‘were made (into men) with arms and heads cut off’.
Perfect of √पा ‘drink’: reduplication प- and the ending -औ of roots in -ā (cf. ययौ, 6.7).
Nominative plural of a bahuvrīhi ending in the s-stem शिरस्: -शिरसः (like सुमनसः).

mantras.anvaya: तथा अपरे तेन विच्छिन्नबाहुशिरसः कृताः। धुतकेसरः (सः) च अन्येषां कोष्ठात् रुधिरं पपौ।

mantras.lit: Likewise others were made by him (into men) whose arms and heads were cut off; and, with mane shaking, he drank the blood from the belly of others.
mantras.tr: Others he left with arms and heads hewn off; and, tossing his mane, he drank the blood from the bellies of others.

comm.t: The lion drinks the blood of the fallen. The image anticipates the next battles, where Kālī and Cāmuṇḍā devour the asuras and drink Raktabīja’s blood (8.59–61).

mantras.lit: In a moment that whole army was brought to destruction by that mighty one — by that lion, the Devī’s mount, exceedingly wrathful.
mantras.tr: In a moment the whole army was destroyed by that mighty lion, the Devī’s furious mount.

comm.t: The sixty thousand of 6.7 are gone in a moment. The general fell to the Devī’s syllable, the army to her lion; she herself does not need to fight further.

samasa.sense: by the Devī’s lion

morph.note: An -ita participle as from a stem क्षयय- (a causative of √क्षि ‘to destroy’, or a denominative from क्षय ‘destruction’). The usual classical causative participle is क्षपित; क्षयित is a Purāṇic form. See Uncertain.

Here the instrumental singular of देवी, agent of निहतम्: ‘slain by the Devī’. The genitive देव्याः would also be written देव्या before n; the instrumental is chosen because it supplies the agent the participle needs, parallel to देवीकेसरिणा in the second line.
Past passive participle of नि + √हन्: the root loses its nasal before क्त (हत). With श्रुत्वा it gives the content of what was heard: ‘having heard (that) the asura (had been) slain’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तम् असुरं धूम्रलोचनं देव्या निहतम्, कृत्स्नं बलं च देवीकेसरिणा क्षयितं श्रुत्वा …
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive clause only: श्रुत्वा with two objects, each with a predicate participle and its agent (असुरं … देव्या निहतम्; बलं … देवीकेसरिणा क्षयितम्). The main verb is चुकोप in 6.21.
mantras.lit: Having heard that the asura Dhūmralocana was slain by the Devī, and the entire army destroyed by the Devī’s lion, then —
mantras.tr: When he heard that the asura Dhūmralocana had been slain by the Devī, and his whole army destroyed by her lion,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues in 6.21; ततः is taken with चुकोप there.

comm.t: The news reaches Śumbha in two parts, which the verse keeps distinct: the general killed by the Devī, the army destroyed by her lion.

flags.uncertain: क्षयितम्: the form is unusual (the classical causative participle of √क्षि is क्षपित); it is kept as printed and analysed as an -ita participle from a stem क्षयय-. देव्या is read as instrumental (agent); a genitive (देव्याः, ‘of the Devī’) is also possible in the written form but leaves निहतम् without its agent.

mantras.anvaya: (ततः) दैत्याधिपतिः शुम्भः प्रस्फुरिताधरः चुकोप, तौ महासुरौ चण्डमुण्डौ च आज्ञापयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause of the sentence begun in 6.20: one subject (शुम्भः) with two verbs, चुकोप and आज्ञापयामास, joined by च.
mantras.lit: Śumbha, the overlord of the daityas, became angry, his lower lip quivering; and he commanded those two great asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa:
mantras.tr: Śumbha, lord of the daityas, was enraged; his lip trembled, and he gave his orders to the two great asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa:

comm.t: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa are Śumbha’s servants who first saw the Devī and praised her beauty to him (5.89–92). Their mission is the subject of chapter 7, which ends with their deaths and the Devī’s new name Cāmuṇḍā (7.27).
A modern reading: Śumbha’s anger grows at each defeat, and with it the force he sends. The quivering lip is the text’s small, exact picture of rage that cannot act on its own.

mantras.lit: O Caṇḍa, O Muṇḍa, surrounded by many forces, go there; and having gone, let her be brought quickly.
mantras.tr: Caṇḍa! Muṇḍa! Take a great force with you and go there; and when you arrive, have her brought here at once.

comm.t: The order is the one given to Dhūmralocana (6.4), now to two commanders and with ‘many forces’. The passive ‘let her be brought’ keeps the king at a distance from the act.

samasa.alt: Also possible as a bahuvrīhi agreeing with असुरैः: अशेषाणि आयुधानि येषां तैः, ‘by (all the asuras) who bear every weapon’. The karmadhāraya, an instrument beside the agent असुरैः, is the more direct reading; the sense hardly differs.

Passive imperative of वि + नि + √हन्: stem हन्य- with the ātmanepada ending -ताम्, ‘let (her) be struck down’. The subject (सा) is carried over from 6.22.

mantras.anvaya: केशेषु आकृष्य बद्ध्वा वा (सा समानीयताम्)। यदि वः युधि संशयः, तदा सर्वैः असुरैः अशेषायुधैः (सा) विनिहन्यताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The two absolutives complete the order of 6.22 (‘bring her, dragging her by the hair or binding her’). Then a conditional clause (यदि … संशयः) and its main clause with the correlative तदा and a passive imperative.
mantras.lit: Having dragged (her) by the hair or having bound (her) — (bring her). If there is doubt for you in the fight, then let (her) be struck down by all the asuras with every weapon.
mantras.tr: Drag her by the hair or bind her, and bring her. If the fight should leave the outcome in doubt, then let all the asuras strike her down with every weapon they have.
mantras.tr_note: The first line depends on समानीयताम् in 6.22; ‘and bring her’ is supplied. यदि वः संशयो युधि, ‘if there is doubt for you in battle’, is taken as ‘if taking her alive proves doubtful’.

comm.t: Śumbha repeats the hair-dragging order (6.4) and adds a fallback: if she cannot be taken, let the whole army kill her. The man who wanted her as the jewel among women (5.100, 5.112) is now willing to see her dead.

mantras.anvaya: दुष्टायां तस्यां हतायां, सिंहे च विनिपातिते, अथ ताम् अम्बिकां बद्ध्वा गृहीत्वा (च) शीघ्रम् आगम्यताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two locative absolutes set the condition; then the impersonal imperative आगम्यताम्, preceded by two absolutives with their object ताम् अम्बिकाम्.
mantras.lit: When she, the wicked one, has been struck down, and the lion felled, then, having bound and seized that Ambikā, let (it) be come back quickly.
mantras.tr: When that wicked woman has been struck down and her lion felled, then seize Ambikā, bind her, and come back at once.
mantras.tr_note: हत ‘struck’ is taken as ‘struck down, overpowered’, not ‘killed’, since she is then to be bound and brought. The impersonal आगम्यताम् is rendered as a command, and the two absolutives are given in natural order (seize, bind).

comm.t: Śumbha’s orders end in contradiction: strike her down (6.23), yet bind her and bring her back (6.24). He wants both her defeat and her person. The chapter closes on the command, and chapter 7 tells how it was carried out. In the Gita Press pāṭha the closing ॐ attached to this mantra belongs to the recitation.

flags.uncertain: हतायाम्: √हन् means both ‘strike’ and ‘kill’. If she is killed, the order to bind and bring her makes little sense, so हता is read as ‘struck down, overpowered’; some translations render it ‘slain’.
